standard: College Board SAT Suite, Reading and Writing section: Standard English Conventions domain, Boundaries skill (joining and separating clauses; comma splices and run-ons)
source: Original content written for Pip, aligned to the College Board's SAT Reading and Writing 'Standard English Conventions' domain (Boundaries skill). All example sentences and quiz items are original; no College Board questions were copied or adapted.
attribution: None required (original content). SAT is a trademark of the College Board, which is not affiliated with and does not endorse Pip; the domain and skill names are cited only to show alignment.
in_scope: joining two complete sentences with a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a FANBOYS word (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so)
spotting and fixing run-on (fused) sentences with no punctuation at all
telling a complete sentence from a fragment
no single comma between who did it and what they did (subject and verb)
why pausing out loud is not a reliable comma rule
out_of_scope: commas in lists and the Oxford comma
transition words like however and therefore between sentences
verb tense, subject-verb agreement and pronouns (the SAT's Form, Structure, and Sense skill)

look_fors: Recognizes when the rule applies: each part ('I was tired', 'I went to bed') is a complete sentence that could stand alone
Names at least one correct way to join them: a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a FANBOYS word
Shows the join on an example
probe_ladder: Then what is allowed between 'I was tired' and 'I went to bed'? I paused there, so I put a comma.
Is 'I was tired' a whole sentence by itself, or does it need more?
Which of these is allowed: 'I was tired. I went to bed.' or 'I was tired, I went to bed.' or 'I was tired, so I went to bed.'?
Then 'I was tired and, I went to bed' is fine, because I paused after 'and'. That's what my rule says.
concepts.friend_nudge: My friend said words like 'and', 'but' and 'so' are little bridges between two sentences…? I don't know what the comma does on the bridge.

look_fors: Says both sides of the comma are complete sentences
Says a comma by itself is not enough to join two complete sentences (a comma splice)
Gives a fix: a period, a semicolon, or adding a FANBOYS word after the comma
probe_ladder: So when is one comma enough by itself, and when isn't it? It's a very nice comma.
Is 'My dog barked, the mail came' one sentence or two? How can you tell?
In 'My dog barked, the mail came', what would you change so it's allowed?
Then 'It rained, we stayed inside' is fine, because I pause there. That's what my rule says.
concepts.friend_nudge: My cousin said a comma is like tape, and you can't hold two bricks together with tape…? I don't know which part is the brick.

look_fors: Says commas follow how the sentence is built (where complete sentences join or separate), not breathing or pauses
Gives a case where a pause and a comma don't match, such as no comma between who did it and what they did
Sorts a tricky sentence correctly (for example, no comma in 'The kid in the red hoodie won the raffle')
probe_ladder: Then how do you find where a comma goes, if not where I breathe?
Do you and I pause in the same places? What if I pause after every word?
Say 'The kid in the red hoodie won the raffle' out loud. I pause after 'hoodie'. Does a comma go there?
Then if I read slowly I get more commas, and if I read fast I get none. That's what my rule says.
spoilers: between the subject and the verb
between a subject and its verb
concepts.friend_nudge: Someone in my class said she covers her mouth and reads the sentence silently to find the commas…? That seems hard to breathe.

offline_demo.note: Yara's SAT Writing run, same beats as the fractions demo: why-question, refusal, real explanation (hit), procedure only (next rung), out-of-scope parking, real explanation (hit), deliberate wrong rule (heal, sets up the k3 quiz miss), re-teach with a new case (level 3, critical). Pip's opening is the server's templated claim from the misconception. 'rung' is the 1-based probe_ladder rung Pip ends the reply on, for 'next_concept_id'. Every quote after 'Saving that:' is a verbatim substring of that turn's student message. All three concepts are kind 'convention': Pip never asks why, only when a rule applies or which of several sentences is allowed.

quiz.pip_answer: The bus was late, so we missed the first bell.
quiz.line: The bus was late, so we missed the first bell. A comma plus 'so'. You said that works.

quiz.pip_answer: No. Two whole sentences joined by only a comma.
quiz.line: No. 'My phone died' and 'I couldn't call you' are two whole sentences, and a comma by itself isn't enough glue.

quiz.pip_answer: The tallest girl on the team, scored twice.
quiz.line: Your rule: put a comma when you take a breath. I took a breath after 'team', so: 'The tallest girl on the team, scored twice.' Now the girl and the scoring are in different rooms. Following your rule anyway. 😵

retry.pip_answer: No comma: The tallest girl on the team scored twice.
retry.line: The tallest girl on the team scored twice. No comma. The who and the what-she-did stay together, even if I need air.
